lessons.title: Ordering
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Mia look at the menu and order their dinner from Sam.

items.example: What would you like to eat?
items.note: The waiter asks 'What would you like?' to politely find out what you want to order.

items.example: I will have the chicken soup, please.
items.note: Say 'I will have…' when you decide what food or drink you want in a restaurant.

items.example: Excuse me, could I have the bill?
items.note: Ask 'Could I have the bill?' when you finish eating and want to pay.

items.example: I would like soup for my starter.
items.note: A 'starter' is a small dish you eat before the big main part of the meal.

image.describe: a small bowl of warm tomato soup with a little piece of bread on a restaurant plate

items.example: For my main course, I will have fish and rice.
items.note: The 'main course' is the biggest and most important dish of your meal.

image.describe: a large dinner plate with roasted chicken, potatoes, and carrots

items.example: We want chocolate cake for dessert.
items.note: Say 'dessert' for the sweet food you eat at the end of a meal.

image.describe: a slice of sweet fruit cake on a small white dessert plate with a fork

grammar.title: Ordering politely with 'I will have'
grammar.explanation: When you choose from a menu at that moment, use 'I will have' (or 'I'll have') plus the food. At the end of the meal, ask politely with 'Could I have the bill?'
examples: I will have the tomato soup.
I'll have chicken for my main course.

practice.explanation: Ask 'Could I have the bill?' when you are ready to pay.

items.example: She loves hot chocolate in winter.
items.note: Hot chocolate is a warm, sweet brown drink made with milk and chocolate.

items.example: Would you like still or sparkling water?

items.example: Can I have my lemonade with ice?

image.describe: clear square ice cubes inside a cold glass of water

items.example: Cheers! Enjoy your drink!
items.note: Say 'Cheers!' when you lift your glass with friends before you drink.

lessons.title: Meat and fish
lessons.scenario: Smarty reads the main courses on the dinner menu in the dining room.

items.example: I will have beef with potatoes.
items.note: Beef is meat from a cow, and we do not count it as one beef or two beefs.

image.describe: a cooked slice of brown roast beef on a dinner plate with vegetables

items.example: We ate roast lamb for dinner.
items.note: Lamb is meat from a young sheep, often served as a warm main course.

image.describe: cooked lamb chops on a white plate with green herbs

items.example: Salmon is my favourite fish.
items.note: Salmon is a pink fish that is very popular in restaurants.

image.describe: a cooked piece of pink salmon fish with a slice of lemon on a plate

items.example: He has two sausages on his plate.
items.note: You can count sausages: say 'a sausage' for one, or 'sausages' for two or more.

image.describe: two cooked brown sausages on a plate next to mashed potatoes

items.example: Do you like pasta with tomato and cheese?
items.note: Pasta is an uncountable food word, so say 'some pasta', never 'a pasta'.

image.describe: a bowl of yellow spaghetti pasta with red tomato sauce on top

items.example: Put some butter on your warm bread.
items.note: Butter is a soft yellow food made from milk, and we say 'some butter'.

image.describe: a small yellow block of butter on a butter dish next to a slice of bread

grammar.title: Countable and uncountable foods
grammar.explanation: Some foods you can count: one sausage, two sausages. Other foods you cannot count: beef, lamb, salmon, pasta, and butter. Use 'some' (not 'a') with uncountable foods.
examples: I would like some pasta and some butter.

practice.prompt: Which word is a pink fish?
practice.explanation: Salmon is a pink fish.

practice.prompt: Match each food word with its type.

practice.prompt: Choose the word that works with 'some' (uncountable).

lessons.scenario: Smarty and his friends taste different foods in the dining room and talk about their flavours.

image.describe: a bowl of red soup with a red chili pepper next to it and tiny steam lines

items.example: These potatoes are too salty.
items.note: Say 'salty' when food has a lot of salt in it.

image.describe: a small salt shaker pouring white salt grains onto a plate of food

items.note: Say 'sour' for a sharp taste like a fresh lemon.

items.example: Dark chocolate can taste bitter.
items.note: Say 'bitter' for a strong, sharp taste that is the opposite of sweet.

image.describe: a mug of dark black drink without sugar or milk

items.example: Is this salmon fresh today?
items.note: Say 'fresh' when food was just made or picked and is not old.

items.example: Can you pass the pepper, please?
items.note: Pepper is a dark spice you shake on food, or a crunchy vegetable.

lessons.title: How much?
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Tom check how much sugar, butter, and fruit they have in the dining room.

items.example: How much sugar do you want in your tea?
items.note: Ask 'How much…?' for things you cannot count, like sugar, water, or butter.

items.example: There is a lot of pasta on my plate.
items.note: Use 'a lot of' for a big amount of countable or uncountable things.

items.example: I only want a little butter on my bread.
items.note: Use 'a little' for a small amount of something you cannot count, like sugar or milk.

items.example: There are a few apples in the bowl.
items.note: Use 'a few' for a small number of things you can count, like apples or sausages.

items.example: There are not many carrots in the soup.
items.note: Use 'not many' with plural countable nouns when the number is small.

items.example: Lemonade has a lot of sugar.
items.note: Sugar is sweet white grains we put in tea, coffee, and cakes.

image.describe: a white ceramic sugar bowl with a small spoon full of white sugar

grammar.title: How much / How many, a little / a few, a lot of
grammar.explanation: Use 'How much' and 'a little' with uncountable things (sugar, butter, water). Use 'How many', 'a few', and 'not many' with countable plural things (apples, sausages, eggs). 'A lot of' works with both!
examples: How much sugar? Just a little.
How many sausages? Only a few—not many.

practice.explanation: 'A lot of' works for big amounts of uncountable foods like pasta.

lessons.scenario: Something goes wrong with Smarty and Mia's order at the restaurant, and they solve it politely.

items.example: Excuse me, this is cold.
items.note: Say 'Excuse me, this is cold' politely when hot food arrives cold.

items.example: Excuse me, there is a mistake on the bill.
items.note: Say 'There is a mistake' when the waiter brings the wrong dish or wrong bill.

items.example: Sorry, I did not order this pasta.
items.note: Say 'I did not order this' when the waiter puts a dish you did not ask for on your table.

items.example: This glass is dirty. Could I have another?
items.note: Ask 'Could I have another?' when you need a clean glass or a new hot dish.

items.example: Oh, sorry about that! I will bring a hot one.
items.note: A polite waiter says 'Sorry about that' when they apologize for a problem.

items.example: Thank you for the bill. Is service included?
items.note: Ask 'Is service included?' to check if the waiter's tip is already in the bill.

grammar.title: Being polite when there is a problem
grammar.explanation: Start with 'Excuse me' or 'Sorry' before stating the problem ('This is cold', 'I did not order this'). Then use 'Could I have…?' to ask nicely for a solution.
